newsitem.title: USA: Beneficiaries come up big winners in Medicare debate.
newsitem.headline: Beneficiaries come up big winners in Medicare debate.

text.p: Congress is poised to enact the most far-reaching Medicare changes in decades, giving seniors a wider array of insurance choices, changing industry payments and ensuring the program's near-term solvency.

Moving beyond the bitter political rhetoric of the 1996 election, President Clinton and Republicans joined hands Tuesday on five-year balanced budget legislation reducing Medicare spending by $115 billion and keeping the program's troubled hospital trust fund in the black until 2007.

Despite bipartisan Senate support, the two sides were unable to agree on controversial long-term changes, including gradually raising the programme eligibility age to 67 from 65 and making affluent seniors pay higher monthly premiums.

Medicare faces a severe funding crunch in the next century as the baby boom generation retires and a smaller workforce is left to support the programme. The budget legislation sets up a bipartisan commission to recomend future structural changes.
While warning Washington cannot afford to dither too long, analysts said it was probably unrealistic to expect lawmakers to tackle politically explosive beneficiary changes now.
"If they had attempted to take on everything at once we probably would have gotten nothing," said Gail Wilensky, a Medicare expert who worked for the Bush administration.
"What we've seen is a shot across the bow. The fact (long-term change) was proposed in a bipartisan way in the Senate sends a very significant signal this is not dead."

Some lawmakers complained Congress had missed a golden opportunity. They griped the bill resorted to accounting slight of hand to protect Medicare's hospital trust fund, which was forecast to go broke in 2001 without changes.
The bill shifts fast-growing home health services out of the trust fund into another part of Medicare.

"I'm very disappointed," said Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm. "By adopting the president's ruse of transferring money ... we create the impression that we have dealt with the problem when in fact we refuse to."

Beneficiaries are the winners under the bill, despite the fact they face higher monthly premiums for Part B doctor's care. Hospitals, managed care, home health and other providers are the losers, facing the brunt of spending reductions.

The measure gives the 36 million seniors in Medicare new options beyond traditional fee-for-service medicine, including a 390,000-person pilot programme of tax-free medical savings accounts and greater use of managed care plans.
It expands preventive services to include mammograms, pap smears, prostate and colorectal cancer and diabetes screening.

Doctors and hospitals would be allowed to band together to form new health care networks serving Medicare patients. Lawmakers expect that option to be especially attractive in rural areas where there are few managed care networks. In a further effort to foster managed care in rural areas, the legislation increases Medicare's minimum payment rate.
Managed care plans would have to meet tougher consumer protections, including appeal rights and emergency care.
Medicare Part B premiums, now $43.80 per month, would be frozen at 25 percent of programme costs. The premium would be gradually increased to cover some home health services.
Marilyn Moon, health analyst at the Urban Institute, estimates that over 10 years premium increases would account for a quarter of all Medicare savings.
